summary:
No Sivas-specific statute, enforcement programme, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the sources assembled for this edition. What a trans visitor to Sivas faces is the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in the province is recorded adding prohibitions of its own.

That framework includes a draft legislative threat at the level of penalty. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years, with participation in same-sex marriage ceremonies or celebrations carrying up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility conditions and repeated evaluation hurdles, and imprison care providers for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the measures.

The settled baseline underneath that draft is older and mixed. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. Against that, no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised, and openly LGBT people are barred from military service under a health regulation that classifies homosexuality as a psychosexual illness.

Enforcement against LGBT assembly is documented and repeated. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions used against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 the Istanbul governorate issued blanket bans against both the LGBTI and the Trans Pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year.

Organisations face dissolution as well as prosecution. In December 2025 a court in İzmir ordered the Young LGBTI+ Association dissolved, finding that it had circulated obscene images incompatible with society's moral values that could encourage or promote LGBT identities. Blanket bans combined with case-by-case prosecutions under Law No. 2911 constitute the enforcement climate that provincial authorities in Sivas operate within.

Two further national indicators round out the picture. Press reports in early 2026 recorded that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of behaviour contrary to biological sex, and Türkiye placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern is national rather than local, and the named units in the sources are Istanbul and İzmir, cited here as illustrations of a countrywide climate rather than as a description of Sivas. A visitor should read the Istanbul Pride bans and the İzmir dissolution order as evidence of how provincial authorities across Türkiye apply national direction, not as isolated metropolitan events.

A gap between statute and practice runs through the record. Conduct has been policed, detained and prosecuted while the enabling package remained a leaked draft, a pattern Human Rights Watch flagged when reporting the 11th Judicial Package in October 2025. The subsequent passage of the 12th judicial reform package in 2026 with its anti-LGBT provisions removed shows the legislative track moving in more than one direction at once, and the two packages are not the same instrument.

Document presentation is the standing checkpoint risk. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification, so any stop by police is an occasion on which a passport gender marker can be compared against presentation, independent of whether any LGBT-specific measure is in force.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Türkiye since 1988 and requires sex reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. There is no administrative route that avoids surgery or judicial approval.

There is no comprehensive statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no general legal claim to invoke in employment, housing, education or services.

Military service is a documented site of exposure. A health regulation defines homosexuality as a psychosexual illness, conscripts who declare it must supply photographic proof, and the resulting unfit report can circulate and fuel discrimination in later public employment and civic life.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Until the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 without its anti-LGBT provisions, the draft measures before the parliament would have removed civil-status recognition of gender change altogether.

Organisation and assembly carry direct legal exposure. The December 2025 dissolution order against the Young LGBTI+ Association in İzmir and the continuing prosecutions of 92 pride participants show that membership, attendance and online posting can each become the basis of state action.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a Sivas governorate or Sivas police directive, a local Pride ban, a local detention of a trans person, or a local institution dealing with trans visitors. Whether such measures exist and are simply unsourced here is unresolved, not established as absent.

The relationship between the leaked 11th Judicial Package reported in October 2025 and the 12th judicial reform package recorded as passing in 2026 is not resolved in these sources. Whether the criminalising provisions were ultimately enacted, amended or abandoned cannot be stated from this inventory.

Whether the early-2026 reported proposal on public advocacy was introduced as a bill, and its status, is not sourced. The claim rests on press reporting rather than on a published text.

Two entries derive from Wikipedia rather than a primary or rights-monitoring source: the 1858 decriminalisation date, the 1988 gender-change route, the military regulation, the 2026 package outcome and the ILGA-Europe ranking. They are consistent with the other material but have not been verified against statute or the original ranking table in this edition.
